Genesis: Rashi explained: "Rabbi Isaac said, etc." I remember clearly when I was a child, I saw a very old, ancient manuscript of Rashi's commentary in which it was written that this statement in the name of Rabbi Isaac that Rashi brings is not mentioned in any midrash or Talmud. Rather, what he said "Why does it begin with Bereishit, etc." this is from a midrash and not the words of Rabbi Isaac. But this Rabbi Isaac was Rashi's father, and he was not a great scholar, and Rashi wished to honor his father and mention him at the beginning of his work. So he said to him: Ask some question and I will write it in your name. And he asked him simply: Why did the Torah begin with Bereishit, etc. Therefore, it is not difficult why he asked in duplicate, because the first question is only for the sake of honoring his father. So I saw written there. However, what he wrote that Rabbi Isaac, Rashi's father, was not a great scholar this is not so, for in the last chapter of Avodah Zarah (75a) Rashi brings an interpretation on the Gemara and these are the words: "The language of my father, my teacher, may his rest be honored, and it seems, etc." End quote. "That you conquered the land of seven nations" the commentators asked: Why would they be called robbers? Behold, Canaan was a slave of Shem, as it is written "And Canaan shall be a slave to them," and what a slave acquires, his master acquires, etc. It seems to me that this is not a difficulty, for if someone gave a slave a gift on condition that his master has no rights in it, the master does not acquire it. And so here, the Holy One Blessed be He apportioned to Canaan specific countries, and to his brother Shem other countries, as is explained in the verses. Therefore, this one has nothing in that of his fellow, and it is like a gift explicitly on condition that neither has anything over the other.
Numbers: *“And they shall harass you”—as the Targum translates, this requires explanation: what did it clarify here, since in Parashat Pinchas it is also written, “For they harass you,” and the Targum translates it the same way as here? Moreover, why does Rashi emphasize “you,” since his explanation is on the word “harass”?
It seems that the word צררו (harass) has two meanings:

1.	One meaning refers to causing distress, such as inflicting suffering through beatings and other troubles. In this sense, the proper wording would be “to you” (לכם) rather than “you” (אתכם), as seen earlier in “For they harass you” (צוררים הם לכם), and similarly in “When you are in distress” (בצר לך), which does not say “when you are in distress yourself” (בצר אותך).

2.	The second meaning is similar to “when you besiege a city” (כי תצור על עיר), meaning to surround it from the outside and prevent escape. In this case, the appropriate phrasing would be אתכם (you) rather than לכם (to you), since it implies direct action against the subject.

At first glance, we might interpret the verse here according to the second meaning, since it says אתכם rather than לכם. However, this is incorrect because a siege implies that the enemy is outside and encircling those inside, whereas here, the enemy is mixed among them, since they dwell in their midst as long as any remain. Therefore, the meaning must be as in the first interpretation—one of suffering—and אתכם here functions similarly to לכם.
This aligns with the Targum, which translates it as “they will distress you” (ויעיקון לכון), rather than using a phrase implying direct action against them (יתכון).

This also explains why in Parashat Pinchas, Rashi did not comment, since there the phrase explicitly says צוררים הם לכם (“for they harass you”), which clearly follows the first interpretation. However, here, where the wording אתכם requires clarification, Rashi needed to address the issue.
This seems to be Rashi’s clear intent.*
